title: The cut-off king
summary: Rook and pawn against rook: cut off the enemy king, count the files and walk the pawn to the Lucena.
part.cut.title: The cut
part.cut.summary: The rook on a file between the black king and the pawn, and the white king climbing with the pawn.
part.count.title: The rule of five
part.count.summary: How many files are enough: the pawn's rank plus the files, and the king that escapes the checks from the front.
part.rank.title: Cutting along a rank
part.rank.summary: The black king kept off the rank in front: the rook goes back and forth and the pawn climbs one square at a time.
part.checks.title: The defender's checks
part.checks.summary: Checks from the side and from behind: the king walks toward the rook, steps in front of the pawn, and then the bridge.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: The rules for your games, the exceptions, and what to do when you are the one defending.
step.t_cut: White to move. The pawn is already on the fifth rank and the white king stands next to it. Black has a simple plan to draw, and you have one move to stop it. What is Black's plan, and what is your move?
step.t_cut.hint1: Imagine it is Black's turn. Where does the black king want to go?
step.t_cut.hint2: The black king wants to reach d7 and then stand in front of the pawn. There is a file it cannot cross once your rook is on it.
step.cut: Rd1. The rook sits on the d-file, between the black king and the pawn, and the black king can no longer step on it: d8, d7, d6, all forbidden. That is cutting off the king. Now the pawn has a single escort, your king, and the black king watches from far away. Almost every win in rook and pawn against rook starts like this: before you push the pawn, lock the enemy king on the other side of a file.
step.late: See why it was urgent. Same position, but Black to move: Kd7. Now the black king goes to e8 or e7, in front of the pawn, and your rook is too late. With the defending king in front of the pawn, the Philidor defence is at hand, and it is a draw. The cut is worth gold, but only to whoever gets there first.
step.d_cut: With the black king cut off, the rest is patience. Watch the white king climb with the pawn beside it.
step.d_cut.m1: Re8. The black rook stands in front of the pawn. It cannot stop the pawn alone, but it will try to bother the king with checks.
step.d_cut.m2: Kf5. The king climbs on the side of the pawn away from the black king.
step.d_cut.m3: Rf8+. Check. The black rook will give every check it can.
step.d_cut.m4: Kg5. The king steps out of check without leaving the pawn. No hurry.
step.d_cut.m5: Re8. The rook goes back in front of the pawn and waits.
step.d_cut.m8: Ke7! The king steps in front of the pawn and attacks the rook on f8 as well. The black rook has to leave.
step.d_cut.m9: Rh8. It goes far away, to check from the side.
step.d_cut.m10: e6. The pawn advances under the king's cover. The black king is still on the other side of the d-file, unable to help.
step.m_cut: Your turn. Cut off the black king and start climbing with your king next to the pawn.
step.m_cut.hint: Rd1 first. Then the king climbs along the f-file, on the side away from the black king.
step.m_cut.done: That is the rhythm: the cut first, then the king climbs, stepping out of the checks without leaving the pawn.
step.t_count: White to move. The pawn is a little further back, on the fourth rank. Cutting off the black king looks right. But on which file, c1 or d1? Only one of them wins.
step.t_count.hint1: Count how many files lie between the black king and the pawn after each cut.
step.t_count.hint2: With the rook on d1 the black king reaches c5, one file from the pawn. With the rook on c1 it stays two files away. Add the pawn's rank to that number.
step.five: Rc1. There is a count the textbooks call the rule of five: add the rank the pawn stands on to the number of files separating the defending king from the pawn's file. More than five usually wins; five or less usually draws. Here the pawn is on the fourth rank. With the rook on c1 the black king is two files away: four plus two, six. A win. It is a rule of thumb, with exceptions, but it is right in most positions.
step.oneFile: And after Rd1? The black king comes to c5, just one file from the pawn: four plus one, five. A draw. The black rook on e8, in front of the pawn, checks the white king every time it tries to climb, and the king has nowhere to hide without leaving the pawn. That is the frontal defence, which has a lesson of its own. Here, just remember: one file of cut-off, with the pawn still on the fourth, is not enough.
step.d_five: This is the rule of five: a d-pawn on the fourth and the black king two files away. Watch how the white king escapes the checks from the front.
step.d_five.m1: Kc4. The king climbs on the side away from the black king, the c-file.
step.d_five.m2: Rc8+. The check from the front, which you already know.
step.d_five.m3: Kb5! The king goes to the b-file. That is why the far side needs room: the king uses two files to escape the checks.
step.d_five.m4: Rd8. The rook attacks the pawn, left on its own.
step.d_five.m5: Kc5. The king comes back, defends the pawn and is one rank higher already.
step.d_five.m6: Rc8+. Another check from the front.
step.d_five.m7: Kb6. The king steps to the b-file again, always climbing.
step.d_five.m8: Rd8. The rook attacks the pawn once more.
step.d_five.m9: Rd1! Now your rook gives up the cut to defend the pawn. It can: the black king is so far away that by the time it arrives, the pawn will be gone.
step.d_five.m10: Kf6. The black king runs toward the pawn, too late.
step.d_five.m11: Kc7. The king attacks the black rook and gets out of the pawn's way.
step.d_five.m13: d5. The pawn runs with the king beside it, and White will reach the Lucena. The two files of cut-off bought the time for all of this.
step.m_five: Your turn, in the position from the start of this part. Pick the right file for the cut and start climbing with the king.
step.m_five.hint: Rc1, the two-file cut. Then the king climbs on the far side: Kf4.
step.m_five.done: Two files of cut-off with the pawn on the fourth: six in the count, and the win is secure. Now it is just the technique you saw.
step.t_rank: White to move. Here the black king is not far away: it is on the same rank as the pawn. But your rook on c5 keeps it off the fifth rank and off the c-file. How do the king and pawn climb without losing that cut?
step.t_rank.hint1: The white king has to climb, and for that it needs a path where the black rook cannot bother it. Where can your rook protect it?
step.t_rank.hint2: The rook goes to the a-file, next to the king. Later, with the king higher up, it comes back to the c-file with check.
step.rank: A king can also be cut off along a rank. With the rook on c5, the black king cannot enter the fifth rank: it cannot get in front of the pawn. When the black king is on the same rank as the pawn, as here, it is called a perfect cut, and it wins with a knight or bishop pawn on any rank. If the black king is already one rank above the pawn, the cut is imperfect and the defence has more chances. The technique is a staircase: the rook goes back and forth between the a-file and the c-file, and with each round the king and pawn climb one rank.
step.d_rank: Watch one full step of the staircase.
step.d_rank.m1: Rc6. The rook moves up one square and stays on the c-file, holding the black king on the other side.
step.d_rank.m2: Rb8. The black rook stands in front of the pawn on the b-file, ready to check from the front when the white king leaves it.
step.d_rank.m3: Ra6! The rook moves to the a-file. Now the white king can climb along the a-file without a check from the front: the rook is there, blocking.
step.d_rank.m4: Kd5. With the rook off the c-file, the black king comes closer.
step.d_rank.m5: Ka4! The king climbs, right next to the pawn.
step.d_rank.m6: Kc4. The black king closes in, hoping to get in front of the pawn.
step.d_rank.m7: Rc6+! The rook returns to the c-file with check and pushes the black king away.
step.d_rank.m8: Kd5. The black king steps back.
step.d_rank.m9: b5. The pawn climbs one square, protected by the king.
step.d_rank.m10: Ra8+. With the a-file open, the black rook checks along it.
step.d_rank.m11: Kb4. The king returns next to the pawn. It is the same picture as before, one rank higher. Now repeat.
step.m_rank: Climb one more step of the staircase. Same idea, one rank higher.
step.m_rank.hint: Rc7, then the rook goes to the a-file. The king climbs to a5, the rook returns to the c-file with check, and the pawn advances.
step.m_rank.done: One more step. One more like it and the pawn reaches the seventh, with the black king still on the wrong side: from there comes the Lucena.
step.t_checks: White to move. The cut worked and the pawn is on the sixth, but the black rook has started checking from the side. Where does your king go?
step.t_checks.hint1: There is no shelter on the black king's side: it is close, and your own rook is over there.
step.t_checks.hint2: Walk toward the black rook. Once the king gets close to it, the checks from the side are over.
step.checks: After the cut, the defending rook has only one job left: giving checks. From the side, it needs distance. So the white king walks toward it: every step closer shortens that distance, and once the king is next to it, the rook has to move. Running to the black king's side would hand over the pawn.
step.d_checks: Watch the white king walk against the checks until it stands in front of the pawn.
step.d_checks.m1: Kf8. The king goes toward the black rook, away from the black king.
step.d_checks.m2: Rh8+. Another check from the side.
step.d_checks.m3: Kg7! The king attacks the rook. The checks from the side are over.
step.d_checks.m4: Rh2. The rook goes far away, to try checks from behind.
step.d_checks.m5: e7. The pawn reaches the seventh.
step.d_checks.m6: Re2. The black rook sits behind the pawn.
step.d_checks.m7: Kf7. The king protects the pawn.
step.d_checks.m8: Rf2+. A check from behind, along the f-file.
step.d_checks.m9: Ke8. The king shelters in front of the pawn. And the black king is still cut off by the d-file.
step.d_checks.m10: Kc7. Black waits. Do you recognise this position?
step.bridge: It is the Lucena position: king on the queening square, pawn on the seventh, black king cut off, and the black rook keeping the white king from leaving along the f-file. You already know how it ends. First Rc1+, to push the black king one more file away. Then the rook to the fourth rank, and the king walks out: when the checks come, the rook steps in the way. That is the bridge. The cut from the very first move brought you here.
step.m_bridge: Finish the job: push the black king one more file away and prepare the bridge.
step.m_bridge.hint: A check on the c-file, then the rook to the fourth rank.
step.m_bridge.done: Rc4. Now the white king walks out, and when the black rook checks, your rook closes the way. From the first cut to the bridge, that is a whole endgame.
step.recap: Three rules. One: cut off the enemy king before anything else, on a file between it and the pawn, ideally with that king on the side with more files. Two: count. The pawn's rank plus the files of cut-off; more than five usually wins. Three: after the cut, the king climbs with the pawn, escapes the checks from the front on the far side and walks toward the rook when the checks come from the side. At the end, the Lucena and the bridge.
step.exceptions: The rule of five has exceptions, and the best known is this one, by Chéron, from 1923: a knight pawn on the fourth and the black king two files away. The count says six, but it is a draw. The knight pawn leaves the white king only one file, the a-file, to escape the checks from the front, and that is not enough. With a rook pawn it is worse still: the black king must be cut off by four files or more. A rule of thumb helps you think, but the position decides.
step.defend: And when you are the defender? Here the colours are swapped: your king is cut off by the black rook on the d-file, two files from the pawn. By the count, Black wins. But it is your move: Kc4, or Kc3, and the king leans on the cut. Now it is a single file, and the frontal defence holds. A defender never lets the king drift away from the pawn: every file counts.
step.finish: Now the practical test. The black king is already cut off, three files from the bishop pawn. Climb with the king, escape the checks on the far side and reach the Lucena.
ex.e05: White to move and win. Your rook keeps the black king away from the front of the pawn. Climb one step of the staircase.
ex.e05.hint: Your rook is already on the b-file, guarding the king's path. First the king climbs; then the rook comes back with check.
ex.e05.solution: Kb4, right next to the pawn, and after Kd4, Rd6+: the rook returns with check and pushes the black king away. Then the pawn climbs one square.
ex.e07: White to move and win. The black king is one rank above the pawn: the cut is imperfect. But it is your move.
ex.e07.hint: The white king has to climb before the black king reaches the pawn.
ex.e07.solution: Ka4 (Ra6 also wins). The king climbs next to the pawn and the staircase goes on. If it were Black to move, Ra8 would draw: with an imperfect cut, one tempo decides.
ex.e09: White to move and win. A position by Capablanca: the black king is two files from the bishop pawn, but the pawn is still on the second rank. Only one move wins.
ex.e09.hint: Do the count for each possible pawn advance.
ex.e09.solution: f4! The pawn reaches the fourth in one move, and four plus two is six. With f3 the count would be five, and Black would have time to set up the checks from the front. After Re8+, the king climbs with Kf3.
key.cut: One file of cut-off with the pawn on the fifth: Rd1 is the only winning move.
key.count: Rule of five: Rc1 wins, Rd1 draws.
key.five: Wikipedia's example of the rule of five (citing Soltis and Mednis): pawn on the fourth, king two files away. Also in bar11319's study on Lichess.
key.villa: A perfect cut along a rank, position 10.17 by Jesús de la Villa, as quoted in Wikipedia.
key.cheron: Chéron's exception (1923), via Wikipedia: a knight pawn, the king two files away, and still a draw.
key.capablanca: A position by Capablanca, via Wikipedia: the pawn reaches the fourth before the black rook can set up the checks from the front.
history: Cutting off the king is the oldest idea in rook endings: textbooks present it even before the Lucena, which is where it leads. Nikolay Kopaev, in a 1958 book, summed up what happens with the pawn on the sixth or seventh: with the defending king cut off by two files or more, the side with the pawn always wins. André Chéron showed the knight-pawn exception in 1923, and Capablanca left an example of how a single tempo decides. The rule of five, the count of the pawn's rank plus the files of cut-off, appears in books by Andrew Soltis and Edmar Mednis, and the staircase of the cut along a rank is in Jesús de la Villa. Today the tablebases confirm all of it, and it fits in one sentence: cut first, count second.
practice: Now the practical test: rook and pawn against rook, with the black king far from the pawn. Keep its king away, climb with yours and take the pawn all the way to promotion.
ex.e11: White to move and win. From the game Pein–Ward, British Championship 1997, with the colours swapped. The black rook cuts your king off along the fourth rank. What is the plan?
ex.e11.hint: The black king is heading for the pawn. Before pushing or bringing your king, ask which file it has to cross.
ex.e11.solution: Re7! The rook leaves the back of the pawn and cuts the black king off along the e-file. (Rc6 also wins.) Pushing at once (c6), bringing the king (Kc3, Kd2) or cutting too close (Rd7) gives the black king time to reach the d-file, and it is a draw. After Kf6, the rook steps back along the same file with Re2 (or Re1, Re8): the cut stays, and the white king has all the time it needs to climb.
ex.e12: White to move and win. A rook pawn: your king is stuck in front of it, and the black king is far away on e7. Get your king out without letting the black king come back.
ex.e12.hint: The king can only get out if the rook covers the b-file. But the rook cannot let go of the black king on its way there.
ex.e12.solution: Rc8!, and after Kd6, Rb8!: the rook reaches the b-file through the eighth rank, and the black king gains no time to come closer. Against Ra1, Kb7!, and the king is out; after Rb1+, Kc8 (Ka6 also works), and the king goes on to d8. With a rook pawn the black king must be four files away or more; here it is, so there is a win, but only along this path: any other move in the first three turns draws.
ex.e13: White to move and win. From the game Uhlmann–Gulko, Niksic 1978, with the colours swapped. The black king is far away, but the black rook watches the pawn. Only one path wins, and it has three only moves.
ex.e13.hint: First force the black rook to stand in front of the pawn. Then use your rook to cut the black king off along a rank, not a file.
ex.e13.solution: e7!, and the black rook has to go to e8. Now Re6!: the rook guards the pawn from behind and cuts the black king off along the sixth rank, far from f7. After Kg5, Ke4! is the only move: the king climbs through the centre, right next to the rook. From there it is the staircase along the e-file: the rook steps down one square (Re5) when the black king comes close, and the white king goes ahead of it until it reaches the pawn.
